🐛 Describe the bug
I am trying to export a transducer decoder network to ONNX using dynamo=True. It fails. Here is a reproducible example:
import torch

def exists(x):
    return x is not None


class TransducerDecoder(nn.Module):

        super().__init__()
        self.embed = nn.Embedding(nclasses+1, embed_dim, padding_idx=nclasses)
        self.dec   = nn.LSTM(embed_dim, hidden_dim, num_layers=1, batch_first=True)
        self.proj  = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
    def forward(self, tokens, h=None, c=None):
        x           = self.embed(tokens)
        x, (h,c)    = self.dec(x, (h,c) if exists(h) and exists(c) else None)
        x           = self.proj(x)
        return x, (h,c)

c       = torch.randn(1,dim)

print("Checking forward pass...")

🐛 Describe the bug
I noticed that when I use aoti_compile_and_package with max_autotune, in certain conditions the result is wrong. Specifically:

It's important to set_num_threads(4). With 1 threads it doesn't reproduce
It's important to do import cv2, without it the bug doesn't reproduce
Adding os.environ['OPENCV_FOR_OPENMP_DYNAMIC_DISABLE'] = '1' before import fixes the issue

My explanation of this behavior is that code produced by max_autotune looks like this
void cpp_CppMicroGemmFP32Vec_threaded_mm(const float* X, const float* W, float* Y, const int64_t ks_b_index)
...
    #pragma omp parallel num_threads(4)
    {
        
        const int tid = omp_get_thread_num();
        const int64_t k_group_id = tid / num_Kt_blocks;
        const int64_t k_slice_id = tid % num_Kt_blocks;
...

and the code relies that this block would be really executed 4 times in parallel. But if you call omp_set_dynamic, openmp can ignore this thread hint and run the code less times that leads to wrong results and this behavior is documented here. Unfortunatly omp_set_dynamic is called while I'm importing cv2 library, specifically here when just loading shared library.
So, I think it should be fixed somehow, to not depend on this kind of OMP behavior, and maybe even use at::parallel_for instead, because different parallelizing backends can be enabled, not necessary openmp
This notebook should reproduce the bug, but I didn't manage to do it in colab because there max_autotune chooses different implementation and pytorch version is also different.
data.zip
On pytorch 2.9 it doesn't reproduce, but I noticed that the generated code is using different constants. Maybe layout of input tensors in BMM has changed, so the bug isn't triggered, but anyway the code still relies on the invariant that actuall executed count is equal to #pragma omp parallel num_threads=N

🐛 Describe the bug
We have found extreme flakiness in this unit test:
python test/inductor/test_compile_subprocess.py GPUTests.test_var_mean_tile_reduction_True_cuda
It comes from a combination of inductor autotuning process and a triton kernel that is sensitive to the block size.
GPUTests.test_var_mean_tile_reduction_True_cuda basically tests torch.compile for
torch.var_mean(x, [1, 3])
with this config:
torch._inductor.config.triton.prefer_nd_tiling=config_val
torch._inductor.config.triton.tile_reductions=config_val
torch._inductor.config.triton.cudagraphs=False # as in check_model_gpu
Please see the minimal torch repro  -> however, this is very flaky and the error might not manifest itself too often.
The resulting triton kernel has this signature:
def triton_per_fused_var_mean_0(in_ptr0, out_ptr2, out_ptr3, xnumel, r0_numel, XBLOCK : tl.constexpr):
    xnumel = 8
    r0_numel = 8
    R0_BLOCK: tl.constexpr = 8
    rnumel = r0_numel
    RBLOCK: tl.constexpr = R0_BLOCK
    ...
If we run this kernel with XBLOCK=1 (resulting in grid (4,1,1)) it works allright.  However, if we try XBLOCK=4 (resulting in grid (1,1,1)), a memory overflow/write happens..!
You can try this for yourself with the minimal triton repro -> the error happens both for CUDA/nvidia and ROCm/amd.
This results in a flaky unit test error, as the inductor autotuning process may sometimes opt for XBLOCK=4.
There are two possiblities here:

The produced triton kernel code is such that it doesn't play along with any other XBLOCK than 1 -> triton code generation bug in pytorch inductor
The kernel code is ok, but there is a bug in the triton compiler that manifests itself only when XBLOCK != 1

🐛 Describe the bug
Description:
When compiling a model using torch.compile, a NotImplementedError: View is raised during in-place mutation when the model contains:
Nested view operations.
Multiple nn.Parameter assignments from intermediate tensors.
In-place operations (e.g., mul_) on parameters.
This seems related to issue #168236, but this reproducer uses a different tensor flow and triggers the error in a more complex scenario.
code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class TestModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(64 * 14 * 14, 128)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(128, 10)
        self.loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = F.max_pool2d(x, kernel_size=2)
        x = self.conv2(x)
        x = F.sigmoid(x)
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)

Description：
TorchDynamo fails to compile a model when indexing a tensor shape using a non-constant torch.tensor index (e.g., shape[torch.tensor(1)]). class DotProductAttention(nn.Module):

        super(DotProductAttention, self).__init__()
        self.embed_size = embed_size
        self.heads = heads
        self.head_dim = embed_size // heads
        assert self.head_dim * heads == embed_size
        self.values = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)
        self.keys = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)
        self.queries = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)
        self.fc_out = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)

        keys = self.keys(keys)

🐛 Describe the bug
I found that current strategy of aten.max.dim may get incorrect indices output if sharded the dim for maximization.
Sample code:
import torch
from torch.distributed.tensor import distribute_tensor, Shard

from torch.testing._internal.common_utils import run_tests
from torch.testing._internal.distributed._tensor.common_dtensor import DTensorTestBase, with_comms


class TestRegisterSharding(DTensorTestBase):
    @with_comms
    def test_max_dim(self):
        mesh = self.build_device_mesh()

        x = torch.randn(4, 4, device="cuda")

        max_value, max_indices = torch.max(x, dim=1)

        dist_x = distribute_tensor(x, mesh, [Shard(1)])

        dist_max_value, dist_max_indices = torch.max(dist_x, dim=1)

        print("x:", x)
        print("max_value:", max_value)
        print("max_indices:", max_indices)
        print("dist_max_value:", dist_max_value.full_tensor())
        print("dist_max_indices:", dist_max_indices.full_tensor())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_tests()
Result:
x: tensor([[-1.6165,  0.5685, -0.5102, -0.9113],
        [-1.1555, -0.2262, -1.2891,  1.0654],
        [-0.7167, -0.5333,  0.2078, -0.9798],
        [ 0.7447, -0.2395,  0.2737,  0.0920]], device='cuda:0')
max_value: tensor([0.5685, 1.0654, 0.2078, 0.7447], device='cuda:0')
max_indices: tensor([1, 3, 2, 0], device='cuda:0')
dist_max_value: tensor([0.5685, 1.0654, 0.2078, 0.7447], device='cuda:0')
dist_max_indices: tensor([0, 0, 0, 0], device='cuda:0')
Each rank gets a shape(4, 1) local tensor to call max.dim in this case, and the local result of max indices is [0, 0, 0, 0]. The framework doesn't process the offset of index, which leads to an incorrect global result when the relavant dim is sharded.
Is there a good way to implement a strategy that supports sharding the index dim?
Versions

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Control flow is typically banned during stream capture to a cuda graph. This is banned because control flow like this will implicitly call item() on x.sum() > 0 to copy the boolean condition from device to host, which does cudaStreamSynchronize():
# suppose x is a tensor on a cuda device
if x.sum() > 0:
    return x
else
    return torch.zeros_like(x)

Thus, control flow today requires the usage of torch.compile with cudagraph trees instead.
However, it turns out that torch.cond() composes nicely with CUDA Graph conditional nodes, because the arguments to torch.cond() map very nicely to the parameters required to construct an IF cuda graph conditional node. torch.cond() takes in functions to execute for both sides of the conditional as direct arguments, allowing us to construct the "child" cuda graphs.
Here is a TODO list of items:

Support cuda graph capture of torch.cond() in eager mode pytorch
Support cuda graph capture of torch.cond() with the cudagraphs backend (not really necessary, but easy enough to add) and the "eager" backend.
Support cuda graph capture of torch.cond() with the inductor backend.
Make sure that autograd works as well.
Use the ELSE statement supported since CUDA 12.8, rather than two IF nodes to implement this, for a small performance boost. Note that pytorch supports only CUDA12.6 and newer right now, so I might require CUDA 12.8 or higher for this feature for simplicity. We will see.

There was an attempt to implement this over a year ago here: #140979
The biggest problem back then was that torch DispatchModes did not support higher order ops, but this was added recently: 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/utils/_python_dispatch.py
    
    
         Line 88
      in
      a3cc252
    
  
  
    

        
          
           supports_higher_order_operators = False 
        
    
  

 Thank you @ydwu4
At this point, I actually rebased that PR #140979 already at https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/galv/cudagraphs-conditional-nodes-4, just to check if Yidi's change fixed my problems, and it does. So there are not likely to be any serious issues at this point with implementing points (1), (2) and (4). I will leave the implementation of (3) as a TODO item for now because I am not familiar with the inductor backend in pytorch.
Some motivation for this:
Firstly, the desire to do basic data-dependent computation has come up several times, but one of the key use cases is skipping the optimizer in the case of a NaN gradient in mixed precision training.
Secondly, figuring out making torch.cond() work with cuda graphs paves the way for adding support for torch.while_loop() in cuda graphs, which may be used to do MoE inside a cuda graph without dropping tokens, but that is more complicated and requires its own issue to write down those issues (they go beyond just while_loop support for cuda graphs; it may also need tricky memory management for autograd).
